Synapse Semiconductor (YC S26) is a frontier semiconductor research lab building senses for physical AI. Led by Sanjeev Chauhan and Duke ECE Faculty Tania Roy . Synapse Semiconductor builds image sensors that process AI on the sensor itself. Each pixel captures light and runs neural-network computation in the same device, replacing the need for a GPU while cutting the power and latency of edge vision. Today - with the launch of RETINA- we are reimagining the core technology for self-driving cars, drones and humanoid robotics. Like the New World once was, space is the next great frontier to explore. In the future, drones will navigate using vision alone, robots will scout the Moon for the next colony, and satellites will perceive their environment and react in real time. At the foundation of it all will be Synapse Semiconductor. book.synapsesemi.org ...more ...more

Today our Deep Learning Applications course had our first "mini" hackathon of the semester. Focusing on computer vision, the challenge was to use data augmentation + transfer learning to help solve a real-world problem in 2 hours. After 2 hours, teams pitched their prototype and the class voted on the winner. From disaster relief to galaxies to skin cancer screening, the teams showed up in a big way. Our winning team found a problem right outside the classroom window - literally! Jaideep A. , Hanfu Zhao , and Keming Zhou built a real-time construction site monitoring system to monitor whether people were wearing a hardhat 👷 and they tested in with a construction crew on the Duke University campus (permission was obtained). During their pitch, Jaideep video-called in to give a live, onsite demo with the Streamlit app they created to test their model in the real world. How cool is that?! 👏 Duke Master of Engineering in AI Product Innovation Duke University Pratt School of Engineering ...more ...more

We are thrilled to announce that iHub - AWaDH @ IIT Ropar has been granted a patent for a impactful invention: "𝐀𝐧 𝐀𝐮𝐭𝐨𝐧𝐨𝐦𝐨𝐮𝐬 𝐒𝐲𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐦 𝐟𝐨𝐫 𝐋𝐨𝐰 𝐏𝐚𝐲𝐥𝐨𝐚𝐝 𝐆𝐫𝐢𝐩𝐩𝐞𝐫 𝐂𝐡𝐚𝐧𝐠𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐌𝐞𝐜𝐡𝐚𝐧𝐢𝐬𝐦 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐈𝐭𝐬 𝐌𝐞𝐭𝐡𝐨𝐝." This patented technology marks a significant milestone in agricultural robotics. The invention features an automatic gripper changing system designed to enhance efficiency and flexibility in agricultural operations. With this system, robots can autonomously switch between different grippers tailored for various crops, all without human intervention. The system comprises a gripper cabinet housing multiple grippers, a robotic arm, and a changing link, which together facilitate seamless gripper transitions. Over the past ten weeks at Veeam, I had the opportunity to build and ship production code as an AI Intern on the Applied AI team! During my time here, I got to work on multiple projects: - MCP Authorization Framework: Built access controls enforcing the subscription tiers for our MCP tools. - Subscriptions Tool: Built an MCP tool surfacing live subscription data directly to AI agents. - MCP Apps: Developed interactive dashboards rendering tabular/JSON data visually inside AI chat clients The highlight was the Intern Summit where I got to meet executive leadership, connect with the intern cohort, and participate in a pitch competition (that my team won!) I would like to thank my manager Lauren Saxton , mentor Sirish Bathina , and the rest of my team for fostering such a supportive learning environment. I would also like to thank Shelby O'Meara , Brooke Vulcano , and Meredith Trotta for making my experience so memorable! #Veeam

Excited to share that I've been given the opportunity to join TraceRoot.AI (YC S25) as a Software Engineering Intern down in San Francisco this summer! I'm especially excited to work at the intersection of AI agents, developer tooling, and infrastructure — building directly with the founder, talking to users, and shipping fast in a startup environment. TraceRoot is building the self-healing layer for AI agents — helping engineering teams trace, debug, and automatically fix agentic systems in production. If your team is shipping AI agents and thinking about reliability or debugging, it's worth checking out. Huge thank you to Xinwei He for this opportunity. Can't wait to get started. If you're in the Bay Area this summer, would love to connect!

I have talked about this book with my Duke adjunct colleagues in engineering. I urge all to read it wearing a moral hazmat suit and with a barf bag in hand. My colleagues in engineering management are, overall, late career, engaged business people who are overall happy people - we teach, we have healthy relationships with adults our age, we have our businesses, and care about the wellbeing of students. It's gross to think of students as our next meal ticket. (The predatory culture Baker describes in his book.) NET: I AM SO PROUD to work with adjunct colleagues in the graduate school of engineering who demonstrate superb care for students - high standards, high encouragement. So many of my colleagues spent their summers listening to struggling students - or happy students - and using our precious unpaid hours to help, listen and support them. When I hear my colleagues perspectives, not one has been "how can this student be my meal ticket" or "I'm off the clock." It's "How can we help in a way that helps them build their character for the future."
